what_its_for: Adalimumab-afzb is used to treat several conditions where your immune system is overactive and causing inflammation. These include rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis (spine arthritis), Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, plaque psoriasis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children. It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes swelling, pain, and damage to your joints and tissues.
how_to_take: Adalimumab-afzb is given as an injection under your skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in your stomach area or the front of your thigh. Your doctor or nurse will show you how to inject yourself at home. Always rotate the injection site each time and avoid areas that are bruised, red, tender, or scarred. Take the pen or prefilled syringe out of the refrigerator about 15 to 30 minutes before your injection and let it warm up to room temperature. Do not shake the pen or syringe. Check the liquid before injecting — it should be clear to slightly yellow with no particles.
dosing: The dose depends on your condition, weight (especially for children), and your doctor's instructions. For most adults, the typical starting dose is 80 mg followed by 40 mg every other week, or as directed by your doctor. Some conditions may require different schedules such as weekly dosing. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, inject it as soon as you remember. Then go back to your regular schedule. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue on your normal schedule. Do not inject two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store adalimumab-afzb in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it, and do not use it if it has been frozen. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 14 days, but once removed from the refrigerator, do not put it back and use it within 14 days. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of used pens and syringes in a sharps container — never throw them in the regular trash.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections while taking this medicine, as it lowers your immune system's ability to fight germs. Do not receive live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine, shingles vaccine Zostavax, or MMR) while on this medication — talk to your doctor about which vaccines are safe for you. Avoid excessive sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine may increase your risk of certain skin cancers. Tell all your doctors and dentist that you are taking this medication before any procedure.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, cough, sore throat, painful urination, or wounds that won't heal; signs of tuberculosis (TB) such as persistent cough, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of your face or throat, trouble breathing, or chest tightness; numbness or tingling in your arms or legs; vision changes; unusual bruising or bleeding; extreme tiredness or pale skin; or new or worsening skin changes such as a rash or unusual moles. Also call your doctor if you notice signs of heart failure such as shortness of breath or sudden weight gain.
when_it_works: Some people start to feel better within 2 to 4 weeks of starting treatment, but it may take up to 3 to 6 months to feel the full benefit of this medication. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you don't notice improvement right away, and don't stop without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Children: This medicine can be used in children as young as 2 years old for certain conditions. The dose is based on your child's weight. Pregnant women: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. This medicine should only be used in pregnancy if clearly needed, as it may affect the baby's immune system. If you take this medicine during pregnancy, your baby should not receive live vaccines for at least 5 months after your last dose during pregnancy. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of this drug may pass into breast milk; discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Elderly patients: Older adults may have a higher risk of infections and should be monitored closely. People with infections or TB: Do not start this medicine if you have an active infection. You will be tested for tuberculosis (TB) before starting treatment.
